biography.name: Tessa Redbird

background.family: Lives with father, grandmother, and younger brother; mother lives across town and remains closely involved.
background.finances: Stable income from municipal maintenance and retail management; careful budgeting covers classes and sports.
background.geography: Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, with extended family in north Texas and planned visits to Texas campuses.
background.cultureLanguages: Citizen of the Cherokee Nation; English-speaking, with family-supported Cherokee language learning and varied participation in community events.
background.school: Public high school with a strong shop program and an after-school newspaper.
background.accessOpportunities: Access to tools, a library, and regional youth events; eligible options and financial support for college are being researched rather than assumed.

timeline.story: Tessa spent afternoons beside her grandmother making picture labels for pantry shelves. She liked deciding what a useful picture needed to show and happily explained the entire system to visitors who only wanted a cup.

She learned to ride a bicycle in a school parking lot and wanted to understand why the chain sometimes slipped. Her father let her turn the pedals while the bicycle stood upside down and watched her test ideas.

A family language class introduced greetings and songs she could practice with her brother. She enjoyed the shared activity but resented classmates later assuming she could translate anything they found online about Native people.

During remote school she repaired two donated bicycles with her father. Sorting usable parts appealed to her, while writing descriptions for the eventual recipients revealed how much knowledge her first explanations had taken for granted.

She joined the newspaper to photograph sports, then discovered an interest in interviewing people who maintained school facilities. Her first article needed major revision because she had collected vivid quotations without explaining what had happened.

Shop class gave her structured practice with safety and measurement. She also attended family language activities less regularly during basketball season, then chose to return without turning a missed month into a permanent abandonment.

Tessa repairs bikes, writes occasional school articles, and plays basketball for pleasure. Family in Texas makes several colleges and technical programs feel geographically imaginable, but she wants to compare actual classes rather than follow the first route an adult suggests.

ambitions: Comparing several educational routes
Imagines an independent place close enough for regular family visits and projects with her brother.

biography.name: Maya Fenwick

background.family: Lives with an aunt and uncle under a stable kinship guardianship, alongside their son; she has supervised contact with her mother when arrangements permit.
background.finances: Modest but reliable household income; guardianship costs reduced savings, and school supplies are planned together.
background.geography: Lubbock, Texas, after several earlier moves within the state.
background.cultureLanguages: White and Mexican American extended family; English at home with some Spanish from her aunt’s relatives.
background.school: Public high school; a counselor coordinates records from previous schools and helps her catch gaps without repeating entire subjects.
background.accessOpportunities: Library access, a supportive dance studio scholarship, and local college outreach provide continuity.

timeline.story: Maya loved making up dance steps with a neighbor and teaching them to anyone who would watch. She also memorized picture-book jokes and delighted in delivering the punch line before adults reached the final page.

Changes in her mother’s housing meant switching classrooms more than once. Maya became quick at spotting which children welcomed newcomers, while sometimes keeping her favorite belongings packed after everyone else considered a move finished.

She stayed with several relatives before settling with her aunt and uncle. A predictable bedtime and permission to keep a lamp on helped, but she still needed time before asking for things she thought might be inconvenient.

Remote school at her aunt’s table revealed uneven math preparation alongside strong reading. Rather than treating everything as missing, a tutor checked specific concepts and helped her build a short, manageable practice routine.

A community dance scholarship gave Maya the same classmates every week. She enjoyed rehearsal and disliked public fundraising stories about her circumstances, so her aunt helped ask organizers to discuss the program without identifying recipients.

She joined the library’s teen advisory group and suggested less formal ways for newcomers to enter meetings. A disagreement about event spending taught her that welcoming people still required decisions that could disappoint someone.

Maya now attends school regularly, dances twice weekly, and helps plan library events. Family contact can still disrupt her concentration, but trusted adults help her recover routines; she is exploring local postsecondary options while allowing herself to imagine staying somewhere by choice.

ambitions: Wants to continue learning after high school
Imagines a predictable home where friends can visit and belongings do not need to stay packed.

biography.name: Sofia Delaney

background.family: Lives with father and younger brother; her mother died from illness when Sofia was twelve, and an aunt remains closely involved.
background.finances: Father’s teaching salary covers a small home; reduced household earnings and medical costs limited savings.
background.geography: Tyler, Texas, with extended family nearby.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American and Irish American family; English at home with Spanish songs and phrases from maternal relatives.
background.school: Public high school; teachers know family circumstances but generally let her decide when to discuss them.
background.accessOpportunities: School art studio, local parks, and an aunt’s transportation support exploration; residential options require careful financial planning.

timeline.story: Sofia spent preschool mornings arranging leaves and pebbles into pretend meals. Her mother photographed some arrangements, and Sofia preferred describing the guests who would eat them rather than naming every plant she had collected.

She began a children’s art class and liked large shared murals better than individual competitions. Her younger brother often interrupted home projects, so they negotiated a separate box of materials he could use freely.

When her mother’s illness changed family routines, Sofia stayed with an aunt more often and learned several simple dinners. She still joined art class and playground games; adults made a point of preserving ordinary childhood activities.

She drew a comic about a family living in a tree during remote schooling. It was funny rather than autobiographical, and her mother helped scan the pages while reminding her that she did not owe anyone a meaningful story.

After her mother died, Sofia alternated between wanting company and wanting privacy. A school counselor and bereavement group offered support, while her father took over household planning instead of treating her as a replacement adult.

She returned to mural projects and began noticing plants along walking routes. Some family anniversaries disrupted concentration, but she learned to request an extension before work piled up; she also started keeping sketches nobody else needed to see.

Sofia paints, walks with her aunt, and helps her brother with occasional homework. She wants to explore education beyond town without assuming distance will resolve grief, and remains undecided about whether her love of collaborative art extends to formal study.

avoids: Being praised for growing up fast
ambitions: Wants room to explore beyond town

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sister; coming out as a trans boy led to conversations and practical changes while family relationships remained affectionate.
background.finances: Stable middle income from bakery management and electrical work; college costs will require comparison and some aid.
background.geography: Albuquerque, New Mexico, with an aunt in El Paso who hosts visits to Texas programs.

background.accessOpportunities: Community gardens, a used-book store, and visits to El Paso make several education and training routes tangible.

timeline.story: Alex liked arranging toy animals into families and drawing maps of their journeys. He wanted bedtime stories repeated until he could tell them himself, then changed one detail to see whether anyone noticed the difference.

He helped his mother roll dough on quiet bakery mornings and enjoyed watching familiar customers greet each other. He disliked the loud mixer, but loved reading handwritten notes tucked beside recipes from older relatives.

A neighbor gave him a small cactus cutting and taught him not to water it constantly. Alex began noticing how patient care differed from constant intervention, and he kept a notebook of changes that were often barely visible.

During remote school he read fantasy novels and exchanged long messages about characters with a friend. He also became more deliberate about his name and clothing, trying possibilities privately before asking others to change how they addressed him.

Alex told his family he was a boy and requested his current name. Most relatives adjusted with practice; his parents helped coordinate school records and protected his choice about who needed personal information beyond the immediate school team.

He volunteered at a community garden and joined a literary discussion group. He liked both plant routines and arguments about unreliable narrators, discovering that a quiet manner did not prevent him from disagreeing firmly when the text supported him.

He now maintains greenhouse plants, reads widely, and visits his aunt in El Paso during breaks. He is curious about continued study but wants to evaluate ordinary daily life on campuses as carefully as their brochures and welcoming statements.

Imagines a home with plants, good books, trusted people, and no need to explain himself constantly.

biography.name: Evan Rourke

background.family: Lives with two parents and a younger sister; family weekends often include grandparents and elaborate board games.
background.finances: Affluent household with tutoring and equipment available, although parents expect him to explain expensive requests.
background.geography: Frisco, Texas, in a car-dependent subdivision.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with Irish American family traditions that matter more to his grandparents than to him.
background.school: Public high school; diagnosed dyslexia is supported through accessible texts, extra reading time, and explicit literacy instruction.
background.accessOpportunities: Can attend Collin College workshops and university open houses across North Texas; family transport and internet are dependable.

timeline.story: Evan narrated complicated rescue stories for toy animals and remembered entire picture books. His parents initially mistook memorized pages for reading and were surprised when unfamiliar words stopped him.

Reading instruction became exhausting, while measuring ingredients with his father felt straightforward. A dyslexia evaluation led to specialized instruction; he worried that leaving class meant everyone thought he was incapable.

Audiobooks let him discuss long novels with his sister. He assembled a marble course over several weekends, recording slow-motion failures, but refused to enter a spelling competition his friends enjoyed.

He made a stop-motion film with neighborhood children. Editing thrilled him; negotiating who could touch the camera did not. A library instructor noticed that he could explain why one cut made a joke work.

He joined robotics expecting constant building and discovered lengthy documentation. Speech-to-text helped, but he still felt conspicuous using it. He left after one season and took up swimming with a cousin.

A history teacher accepted a carefully sourced audio documentary alongside written notes. Evan spent days revising its sequence. He also began cooking full meals, though he abandoned several ambitious recipes when cleanup accumulated.

He films swim meets and is trying robotics again with a smaller team that shares documentation duties. His grades are solid, yet he describes himself as behind whenever classmates finish reading first; unfamiliar practical work sometimes restores his confidence.

timeline.story: Hana made pretend shops from food containers and insisted customers receive tiny paper receipts. She also enjoyed climbing low trees, surprising adults who remembered her mostly as a child who liked tidy indoor games.
Her aunt taught her basic stitching, and she made uneven bags for stones collected in the park. She liked stories read aloud but resisted performing them for visiting relatives.

She helped at a community food distribution day, first sorting cans and later asking visitors what they needed. The conversations interested her more than she expected, although she was tired afterward.

A bicycle puncture became a weekend repair lesson with her father. She preferred the practical puzzle to riding long distances. At school she joined a book discussion group and changed her opinion when another student defended an unpopular character.

She tried theater lighting, found the equipment interesting, and left because rehearsals conflicted with family evenings. An accounting elective appealed because errors could be tracked, but she disliked exercises with no connection to actual decisions.

Trail volunteers taught her to mend drainage channels and identify invasive plants. She enjoyed the muddy work and began recording supply costs. Friends joked that she could turn any outing into a spreadsheet, which was partly true and sometimes annoying.

Hana now alternates service shifts and trail days, occasionally helping her aunt price handmade items. She wants to explore subjects beyond familiar community settings. She is unsure whether her satisfaction comes from nature, practical coordination, or seeing a useful result with other people.

background.school: Public high school; juvenile idiopathic arthritis is supported with flexible seating, extra passing time, and remote participation during significant flares.

timeline.story: Malik liked running obstacle courses and arranging his mother's scarves into costumes. Adults remember him as a child who could turn a cardboard box into a stage within minutes.

He developed joint pain and was eventually diagnosed with juvenile arthritis. Treatment and physical therapy became familiar routines. He kept playing with friends, though he sometimes needed to stop earlier than everyone else.

A flare interrupted a soccer season. While resting, he began editing photos and designing outrageous haircuts on printed portraits. He returned to recreational kicking later but no longer wanted the team's schedule.

He helped a neighbor make posters for a yard sale and discovered that readable prices mattered more than dramatic fonts. Standing all morning was tiring, so he redesigned the table setup to work seated for part of the event.

An introductory coding class bored him until he could change a page's appearance. He enjoyed visual experimentation but found debugging tedious. At a family event he confidently introduced speakers while sitting on a high stool.

He began assisting with hair and costume preparation for school performances, using adapted grips on difficult days. He also liked chemistry lessons about mixtures, although his actual laboratory experience remained limited to ordinary school experiments.

Malik designs publicity for a student production and helps plan seating for audience members with access needs. His symptoms fluctuate. He wants opportunities that allow flexibility without assuming his interests must stay indoors or that every activity should be easy.

openQuestions: Which activities remain satisfying during symptom changes?
Does his interest in chemistry persist beyond visually striking experiments?

He began photographing insects with a borrowed phone and drawing labels in both languages. Reading aloud was enjoyable when the audience was his sister; formal school presentations made him speak very quickly.

A teacher showed him basic video editing. He made a funny family cooking clip and discovered that relatives disagreed about what should be shared. He learned to ask before posting and kept several favorite recordings private.

Family worries occupied more adult conversation, and he noticed changes without understanding the legal situation. He kept playing soccer and started helping his sister organize school materials, appreciating routines that felt manageable.

His mother's removal separated the household across countries. Video calls sustained their relationship but did not replace everyday contact. A school liaison helped his father arrange communication with teachers, while an uncle made sure Diego could continue soccer.

Diego joined media club and made a short film about bus stops rather than family separation. He enjoyed framing ordinary places on their own terms. He also tried electronics repair, becoming competent at replacing a controller cable with supervision.

He balances school, sibling pickup, and weekend soccer. He has begun mapping shaded walking routes for a class project and is unsure whether he likes the technology, neighborhood conversations, or the visual choices most. background.school: Public high school with mock trial, robotics, choir, and ordinary laboratory science.
background.accessOpportunities: El Paso Community College events, UTEP outreach, libraries, and desert education programs are nearby; business shifts limit some weekends.

timeline.story: Micah liked making up trials in which stuffed animals argued about missing snacks. He was equally happy quietly arranging his sister's old costume jewelry into patterns, a habit adults rarely saw outside home.

He helped count inexpensive parts at the family shop and enjoyed asking what each item did. He disliked greasy equipment and learned that understanding a catalog did not require wanting to work on an engine.

A choir director noticed his sense of rhythm, and he liked the group sound. He also read mystery stories alone, often guessing an ending confidently and then defending the wrong guess long after new clues appeared.

He tried robotics with a friend and enjoyed building but lost patience with code. A teacher gave him a short public explanation to deliver; he sounded confident despite relying heavily on a teammate's understanding of the software.

Mock trial gave him enjoyable scripts and arguments. He began noticing that listening carefully could be more useful than speaking first. At the shop he learned to ask customers clarifying questions instead of guessing what they needed.

Micah left robotics for a season, then returned for a design challenge with more hands-on assembly. He made simple jewelry from discarded safe materials at home and showed it to friends only after they asked about a bracelet.

He balances mock trial, occasional choir projects, and shop shifts. A desert field outing has made him curious about outdoor science, though he has little camping experience. He is increasingly willing to say that an appealing possibility is something he has not actually tested.

avoids: Long coding tasks with no visible change
motivations: Understanding rather than merely sounding convincing
Keeping private creativity alongside public activity
ambitions: Try a supervised overnight outdoor program

struggles: Can defend first impressions too long

biography.name: Jordan Keene

background.family: Lives with their mother and stepfather; visits their father during school breaks.
background.finances: Stable moderate income; medical and school supports are budgeted.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family; involved in a welcoming community choir.
background.school: Public high school; documented dyslexia and reading accommodations since age nine.
background.accessOpportunities: Audiobooks, accessible course materials, and a supportive learning specialist.

timeline.story: In 2014, Jordan learned songs quickly and invented endings to familiar stories. They loved being read to and often asked to hear a chapter twice, especially when a character made a confusing decision.

During first grade in 2016, printed directions became a source of arguments. Jordan could explain an experiment aloud but sometimes copied the wrong line, and adults initially treated the uneven work as carelessness.

In 2019, an evaluation identified dyslexia. Audiobooks and explicit reading instruction reduced nightly battles. Jordan remained embarrassed about reading aloud in front of classmates while eagerly volunteering to explain a terrarium they had assembled.

In 2020, remote schooling made some materials easier to enlarge and replay, but inaccessible scanned worksheets still took too long. Jordan and their mother learned to request editable files before an assignment became overdue.

By 2023, Jordan was singing with a community choir and building simple props for performances. They befriended another student through repairing a broken music stand, discovering that shared work made introductions less awkward.

During 2024 and 2025, they helped record oral histories with older neighbors. They listened closely and noticed contradictions between interviews, then worked with a partner to turn their audio notes into carefully checked captions.

At sixteen in 2026, Jordan is investigating accessibility offices at Texas colleges and a local fabrication certificate. They want to compare actual course materials before visiting, and they are still deciding how openly to discuss their reading needs. They recently tested an audiobook platform with their specialist rather than relying on its advertised features.

ambitions: Study away from home with reliable access
Keep performing with others
They imagine an independent home with accessible routines, room to make things, and people to sing with regularly.

biography.selfDescription: I can hear when a story does not quite add up, even when I need extra time to read the transcript. I like working with people who let me show what I mean before deciding what I can do.

biography.name: Malik Thompson

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepfather; older sister attends a Texas college.
background.finances: Steady middle income; travel and access costs require planning.
background.geography: Tacoma, Washington; sister and aunt live near Denton, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: ASL and written English; Deaf community involvement and hearing extended family.
background.school: Public high school; Deaf student with interpreters and accessible media arrangements.
background.accessOpportunities: Deaf youth programs, captioned resources, and relatives supporting Texas visits.

timeline.story: In 2014, Malik enjoyed large block structures and energetic pretend cooking with his sister. His mother used ASL with him, and he loved stories that transformed an ordinary kitchen spoon into several different dramatic characters.

At six, he entered a mainstream classroom with interpreting support. During 2017, he befriended two classmates through drawing games, while family and school worked to make incidental classroom announcements as accessible as formal lessons.

In 2018, Malik joined a Deaf youth outdoor group and tried kayaking. He liked watching the water change around the boat, though he preferred planned routes to open-ended paddling competitions that some other children enjoyed.

During 2020, inaccessible video captions sometimes interrupted online learning. Malik learned to report specific problems and also began making short signed comedy clips with friends, enjoying visual timing and collaborative revision across several takes.

At twelve, he took an introductory design class and became interested in wayfinding. In 2023, he photographed confusing entrances around the city and compared his interpretations with those of friends who noticed entirely different obstacles.

Across 2024 and 2025, Malik helped plan an accessible recreation event and joined a school chess group despite disliking chess competitions. He enjoyed informal analysis, while the event taught him how often an apparently small access detail affected participation.

At sixteen in 2026, Malik is exploring Texas campus visits near his sister and asking specific questions about interpreting and captioning. He wants access to both Deaf peers and broad electives, without assuming one campus feature can answer every daily-life question.

avoids: Being treated as the automatic access spokesperson
ambitions: Visit several different campus settings
He imagines an adult community with easy communication, close friends, and opportunities to explore new places.
practicalConstraints: Access quality must be checked in context

biography.name: Rowan Mercer

background.family: Lives with their mother, father, and younger brother; one parent’s military service has prompted several planned moves.
background.finances: Steady military pay and benefits; family saves for education while tracking possible transfers.
background.geography: Killeen, Texas, after living in Virginia and Colorado.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking, nonreligious family; friendships span several regions and online group chats.
background.school: Secular homeschool program with online courses and a local co-op; chosen partly to maintain curriculum continuity through moves.
background.accessOpportunities: Has base recreation facilities and library resources, but starting new friendships repeatedly can limit participation.

timeline.story: Rowan liked making tiny towns from boxes and dictating rules for their imaginary residents. Their mother preserved photographs before packing, helping Rowan see that an activity could matter even if the structure could not move.

A move to Colorado brought snow and new neighbors. Rowan learned to sled, then spent indoor afternoons designing board games whose rules changed whenever younger children found an unexpected way to win them.

Online classes fit a later relocation, but Rowan missed spontaneous playground contact. A co-op board-game afternoon became important because the same people returned and nobody needed to summarize their entire history each week.

During remote activities they organized a family video-call game night with cousins in several states. Technical problems annoyed them, yet they learned to keep a simpler backup game ready rather than cancel when one tool failed.

In Texas they tried archery through a recreation program and appreciated patient repetition. They also experimented with different clothes and they/them pronouns, finding most family conversations supportive even when relatives needed reminders.

Rowan helped a co-op group create a tabletop mystery. Writing clues was enjoyable, but testing showed that players interpreted them differently; Rowan cut a favorite scene to make the shared experience less confusing.

They now study history and algebra online, practice archery, and maintain a distant friend group. They are comparing local dual-credit options with residential possibilities and wondering what it would feel like to choose a location without already knowing a departure date.

ambitions: Considering dual credit and residential study
Imagines a lasting home base with space for visiting friends and occasional travel.
struggles: Uncertain timing of the next transfer

biography.name: Noah Gentry

background.family: Lives with his grandmother under a stable kinship-care arrangement; his mother is in sustained substance-use recovery and contact has become more predictable over the past year.
background.finances: Limited fixed income supplemented by an aunt; essentials are stable, but optional expenses require advance saving.
background.geography: Lufkin, Texas, after earlier moves between relatives in East Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family with church ties and several distinct views about forgiveness and privacy.
background.school: Public high school; a counselor and designated teacher provide continuity without requiring him to discuss family history publicly.
background.accessOpportunities: Angelina College events, a library, and a community recreation center are accessible when school or relatives provide rides.

timeline.story: Noah liked building towers and giving toy animals elaborate names. His mother read to him regularly, and he remembers the funny voices more clearly than the stories' endings.

He learned to swim at a recreation center and became proud of floating without help. A classroom plant project interested him, although he forgot watering until the teacher put a visible chart beside the pot.

Adult routines became less reliable during his mother's substance use. He stayed with relatives for stretches and learned to pack a familiar book. He still enjoyed school jokes and swimming when someone could take him.

Moves between relatives interrupted attendance and friendships. Adults eventually established care with his grandmother, who handled practical decisions. A school counselor helped him settle; nobody expected him to repair the adults' situation or explain it to classmates.

Predictable meals, transport, and bedtimes made room for ordinary interests again. He joined a garden group and discovered he liked compost experiments more than decorative planting. Swimming returned as recreation rather than another achievement to pursue.

Noah began helping at a community pool's supervised family days and learned to greet visitors. He was not yet qualified for safety responsibility. His mother's recovery brought hopeful contact and some uncertainty; his grandmother maintained boundaries and discussed changes before they happened.

He studies biology, helps with the community garden, and enjoys swimming with friends. He is curious about photography but has only used a phone. Stable routines support his participation, while sudden plan changes can still make him withdraw before asking what actually happened.

motivations: Trying something simply because it interests him
ambitions: Borrow a camera and complete a small photo series
He imagines an adult home with predictable routines, friends welcome at the table, and space to make his own plans

biography.name: Gabriel Soto

background.family: Lives with his mother and aunt; an older cousin nearby is his usual sounding board.
background.finances: Modest but predictable household income; optional purchases and trips need advance saving.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas, in a neighborhood with several generations of extended family nearby.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses English and Spanish daily, reading more quickly in English; family members often disagree vigorously over dinner.
background.school: Public high school with a small discussion club and a library he uses during lunch.
background.accessOpportunities: Internet is reliable, but there is one shared laptop. His aunt attended college and can explain some procedures, although she is often unavailable during the week.

timeline.story: Gabriel asked adults why signs on the same street used different words for similar things. He liked being read stories with repeated phrases and corrected anyone who skipped one. He was also impatient with puzzles, sometimes pushing pieces together until his aunt persuaded him to look at their shapes.

He liked a classroom game where children decided whether a statement about an animal could be true. He would bring up exceptions long after everyone else moved on. During a school performance he forgot a short line and became determined to avoid the next performance, despite enjoying rehearsals with friends.

A disagreement about a game rule led him to read the entire instruction booklet and mark the relevant sentence. He won that argument but discovered his cousin no longer wanted to play. Around the same time he became enthusiastic about drawing maps, then stopped when he found shading them tedious.

Gabriel read two conflicting explanations of a local water restriction and asked his aunt which details each left out. She encouraged him but grew tired of discussing it every evening. He began writing paragraphs in a notebook, enjoying the chance to revise a sentence before anyone could respond.

In class he wrote a careful response to a disputed school rule and was upset when a teacher said his tone sounded contemptuous. He revised it reluctantly. He tried a speaking competition once, disliked waiting under the lights, and found that remembering his points did not prevent his voice from shaking.

He joined a discussion club that allowed written contributions. He compared competing claims about a community issue, separating the factual disagreements from different priorities. Friends appreciated his explanations but sometimes wanted him to stop correcting minor wording. He also took up casual jogging because it required little conversation or equipment.

Gabriel is writing a longer piece about a contested school policy, checking quotations against original documents when he can find them. He enjoys constructing a reasoned argument and dislikes imagining himself presenting it aloud. He has delayed sharing the draft because one missing fact bothers him, and he knows he may be using that gap as cover.
